I formalized some results in non-archimedean functional analysis (NAFA) https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21734, and now I'm considering contributing them to mathlib.

A fundamental notion of this project is "spherical completeness". For any metric space, it means that any descending chain of non-empty closed balls has a non-empty intersection. In my project, this is formalized as follows:

class SphericallyCompleteSpace (α : Type*) [PseudoMetricSpace α] : Prop where
  nonempty_iInter_of_antitone : ∀ ⦃ci : ℕ → α⦄, ∀ ⦃ri : ℕ → NNReal⦄,
    Antitone (fun i ↦ closedBall (ci i) (ri i)) → (⋂ i, closedBall (ci i) (ri i)).Nonempty

For NAFA, this definition is already useful enough. However, spherical completeness is not only useful in NAFA, but also in p-adic geometry (for example, the Berkovich unit disc has no point of type IV if the base field is spherical complete), and it is related to the model theory of valued fields.

The subtlety appears when one considers valued fields. The valuation function does not necessarily induce a metric, especially when the valuation has rank higher than 1. However, the spherical completeness can still be formulated by considering "generalized metric spaces", i.e., a set with a distance function that takes values in a certain ordered structure, instead of NNReal.

This is a reasonable mathematical solution, but maybe not the best one for Mathlib. The PR that attempts to touch the definition of MetricSpace may take forever to be merged, especially when the only current motivation to do so is to deliver spherical completeness.

After a discussion with @Riccardo Brasca , we (mostly, he) found some articles (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1810.09275, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.09930)that deal with exactly the problem. In these articles, the notion of ball space is introduced. It is simply a set X with a family of subsets of X (called the balls in X), nothing more. This is extremely easy to formalize:

class BallSpace (X : Type u) where
  IsBall : Set X → Prop

And it is not hard to show that metric spaces and valued fields are ball spaces. 

instance (X : Type*) [MetricSpace X] : BallSpace X where
  IsBall B := ∃ (x : X) (r : ℝ), B = Metric.closedBall x r

(I'm really having difficulty to play with the valuation related part of mathlib, so let me skip the code and state it informally: a closed ball in a valued field (F,v), where v is an additive valuation with value group G, is a set of for form {x\in F| v(x,a)\geq r} for some x\in F and r\in G.

With ball spaces, the spherical completeness can be restated as follows:

class SphericallyCompleteSpace (X : Type*) [BallSpace X] : Prop where
  nonempty_sInter_of_isChain :
    ∀ S : Set (Set X), S.Nonempty → (∀ B ∈ S, BallSpace.IsBall B ∧ B.Nonempty) →
      IsChain (· ⊆ ·) S → (⋂₀ S).Nonempty

And this definition recovers the original spherical completeness for metric spaces:

theorem Metric.sphericalCompleteSpace_iff {X : Type*} [MetricSpace X] :
    SphericallyCompleteSpace X ↔
      ∀ ⦃ci : ℕ → X⦄, ∀ ⦃ri : ℕ → NNReal⦄,
      Antitone (fun i ↦ closedBall (ci i) (ri i)) → (⋂ i, closedBall (ci i) (ri i)).Nonempty

(LLM proved this for me)

So, ball spaces provide a playground to state the spherical completeness in full generality. But what about the proof? Basically, all the real applications of spherical completeness use the strong triangle inequality (including valued fields with valuation of higher rank). So in this sense, we really need "center" and "radius" of balls, which brings us back to "generalized metric spaces".

After all, I'm not sure what the best solution is for delivering spherical completeness and its applications in Lean (and Mathlib).
How about a middle ground and defining it on uniform spaces and making a claim about docs#UniformSpace.ball ? (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166864114000753)
I have/had some branch/PR trying to generalize IsUltrametricDist to IsUltraUniformity (https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.09722 and van Rooij) which is also relevant if one takes the uniform space route

For your challenge about linking valuations to metric spaces, I'd be happy to discuss with you and understand what's limiting in IsValuativeTopology. Which formulation would be easiest to link up to be able to state and prove: spherically complete iff maximally complete as defined by no proper immediate extensions"? We don't currently have a definition of immediate extension BTW.

In your paper and repo formalizing spherical completeness, you also identified a gap in Schikhof's argument and iirc proposed a new typeclass (radius of ball matches its diameter) that facilitates the proof of spherical completeness for some spaces. How does that one fit it -- what existing types do you propose get instances of BallSpace and the other classes?

The concept of spherical completeness is geometrical rather than topological.

That's from https://www2.physics.umanitoba.ca/~khodr/Publications/2018-Barria-Shamseddine.pdf which I think you cite in your formalization paper. Is there some geometric meaning we'd want to give via BallSpace?
The problem is to link valuation with metric spaces. If the valuation is not of rank 1 the obvious function one can use to define balls is not real valued.

Right, but to create a uniform space isn't a problem for valuations of any rank, because the entourages are { p : K × K | v (p.1 - p.2) < (γ : Γ₀) } for Γ₀ = docs#ValuativeRel.ValueGroupWithZero
If we can define spherical completeness for any uniform space then it seems this would solve the problem. Are you claiming that any uniform space is a balled space in the above sense?

Conceptually, I am proposing extending docs#WithZeroTopology.topologicalSpace to also provide a uniform space, and have a propeq uniform space on things that are IsValuativeTopology via the induced space through the uniform continuous map valuation. We don't have to implement it this way, because this has some of the flaws that Valuedhad.

I am proposing that any uniform space already has docs#UniformSpace.ball and IIUC that can be used to define a balled space. I don't understand all the axioms we require of a balled space, however.
If everything works for uniform spaces I don't think there is any need to introduce a new class.

What's not clear to me is if the other ball spaces discussed in the papers you found, that deal with fixed points etc, can be implemented as ball spaces via the formalism of uniform spaces / entourages.

FWIW Opus gives the following two examples of topologies on the naturals: one is d(x,y)=1 for x!=y, and the other is d(x,y)=1+1/(1+min(x,y)) for x!=y. Both easily checked to be metrics, both induce the discrete topology and also the discrete uniformity (so in particular the same uniform space), but the d(x,y)=1 one is spherically complete whereas the ball centre n radius 1+1/(n+1) is [n,infty) for the other metric, meaning that it's not spherically complete.

In particular, same uniformity but different balls.

Ah yes, that Frechet space counterexamples is something I'd worked with before and should have recalled. So I retract the uniform space proposal.

But then these two examples show that BallSpace Nat also has no obvious canonical definition (intervals?). Why should BallSpace implied by a PseudoMetricSpace be the closed balls and not let's say open balls?

Then I propose, similar to how we discuss local fields limited to nonarchimedean ones, for pragmatic purposes, we associate spherical completeness with ValuativeRel for now, to be able to discuss higher rank valuations, but to the exclusion of the more arbitrary ball spaces as cited in the found papers. This is so that one doesn't have to make a "data" choice for instantiating a BallSpace.

We don't really have a proper definition of "ball space yet" -- is there one? Sure we can claim that a collection of subsets are "balls" but what properties are these things supposed to have?

To avoid diamonds that would come from propeq BallSpace, like from metric closed balls over a NA field and from the le valuation sets... Perhaps we have lowercase sphericallyComplete a property of Set (Set X) or indexed families of Set X. And a global IsSphericallyComplete prop class that is sphericallyComplete metric closed balls over a PseudoMetricSpace. And to support higher rank valuations, we have ValuativeRel.sphericallyComplete also a prop (not necessarily a class).

This avoids data level diamonds for existing use cases, and also allows for statements in the future about ball spaces that are not from such nonarchimedean settings.
Honestly, I still think a generalized metric is the best solution: as it covers most cases that we are interested in.

The problem is the interaction with the (huge) already existing metric library. We can try to have a new class and then slowly generalizing what we already have to this setting. Do you have a concrete definition we can test?
An implementation challenge with a generalized metric, that we ran into with Valued, is that the codomain is underspecified.

import Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace.Basic
import Mathlib.Data.SetLike.Basic
import Mathlib.Order.Filter.Basic

/-
A minimal abstraction of spherical completeness which works uniformly
for metric spaces, valued fields, and general "ball spaces".

The idea:
• A BallFamily is just a set of subsets of α.
• Spherical completeness is a property of such a family.
• For metric spaces, we instantiate BallFamily with closed balls.
• For generalized metrics, we instantiate with balls valued in Γ.
• A descending chain of balls induces a filter; spherical completeness
  is equivalent to this filter being nontrivial.
-/

/-- A family of "balls" in `α`. -/
def BallFamily (α : Type*) := Set (Set α)

/-- A descending chain of balls induces a filter. -/
def chainFilter {α : Type*} (S : Set (Set α))
    (hchain : ∀ ⦃B₁ B₂⦄, B₁ ∈ S → B₂ ∈ S → B₂ ⊆ B₁ ∨ B₁ ⊆ B₂) :
    Filter α :=
  { sets := { U | ∃ B ∈ S, B ⊆ U }
    , univ_sets := by
        classical
        rcases S.nonempty with ⟨B, hB⟩
        exact ⟨B, hB, subset_univ _⟩
    , sets_of_superset := by
        intro U V hU hUV
        rcases hU with ⟨B, hB, hBU⟩
        exact ⟨B, hB, fun x hx => hUV (hBU hx)⟩
    , inter_sets := by
        intro U V hU hV
        rcases hU with ⟨B₁, hB₁, hB₁U⟩
        rcases hV with ⟨B₂, hB₂, hB₂V⟩
        have h := hchain hB₁ hB₂
        rcases h with hsub | hsub
        · exact ⟨B₂, hB₂, by intro x hx; exact ⟨hB₂V hx, hB₁U (hsub hx)⟩⟩
        · exact ⟨B₁, hB₁, by intro x hx; exact ⟨hB₁U hx, hB₂V (hsub hx)⟩⟩ }

/-- Spherical completeness for a family of balls via the induced filter. -/
def SphericallyCompleteFamily {α : Type*} (𝔅 : BallFamily α) : Prop :=
  ∀ (S : Set (Set α)),
    S ⊆ 𝔅 →
    S.Nonempty →
    (∀ ⦃B₁ B₂⦄, B₁ ∈ S → B₂ ∈ S → B₂ ⊆ B₁ ∨ B₁ ⊆ B₂) →
    (chainFilter S ‹_›).neBot

/-- The standard closed balls in a pseudo metric space. -/
def closedBallFamily (α : Type*) [PseudoMetricSpace α] : BallFamily α :=
  { B | ∃ (c : α) (r : ℝ), B = closedBall c r }

/-- Spherical completeness for a pseudo metric space via its closed balls. -/
def SphericallyCompletePseudoMetricSpace (α : Type*) [PseudoMetricSpace α] : Prop :=
  SphericallyCompleteFamily (closedBallFamily α)

/-- A generalized (pseudo)metric space with distances valued in `Γ`. -/
class GeneralizedPseudoMetricSpace (α : Type*) (Γ : Type*) :=
  (dist      : α → α → Γ)
  (zero      : Γ)
  (le        : Γ → Γ → Prop)
  (le_refl   : ∀ x, le (dist x x) zero)
  (symm      : ∀ x y, dist x y = dist y x)
  (triangle  :
    ∀ x y z, le (dist x z) (max (dist x y) (dist y z)))

/-- Closed balls in a generalized pseudo metric space. -/
def gClosedBall {α Γ : Type*}
  [GeneralizedPseudoMetricSpace α Γ]
  (c : α) (r : Γ) : Set α :=
  { x | GeneralizedPseudoMetricSpace.le
          (GeneralizedPseudoMetricSpace.dist x c) r }

/-- The family of closed balls in a generalized pseudo metric space. -/
def gClosedBallFamily (α Γ : Type*)
  [GeneralizedPseudoMetricSpace α Γ] : BallFamily α :=
  { B | ∃ (c : α) (r : Γ), B = gClosedBall (α := α) (Γ := Γ) c r }

/-- Spherical completeness for a generalized pseudo metric space. -/
def SphericallyCompleteGeneralizedPseudoMetricSpace
  (α Γ : Type*) [GeneralizedPseudoMetricSpace α Γ] : Prop :=
  SphericallyCompleteFamily (gClosedBallFamily α Γ)

I've been following this discussion closely, and I'd like to propose an unconventional solution that I believe solves the problem more fundamentally. Please excuse my English — Russian is my native language, and I'm using a translator to convey my ideas as precisely as possible.

Instead of generalizing BallSpace or metrics, I suggest looking at the problem from a different angle: every ball carries information about how it was constructed. It is not merely a subset — it is a pair (center, radius) with a type attached to the radius.

The problem with current approaches:

BallSpace loses the center and radius → we cannot prove properties that depend on structure.

UniformSpace cannot distinguish metrics with the same uniformity (Kevin's counterexample with ℕ).

Generalized metrics require redefining the entire MetricSpace library.

My proposal: structural indexing of balls

Instead of fixing the radius type, we parametrize the entire family of balls by an index type. But the key insight is that the index is not just a value — it is an expression that preserves its identity throughout computations.
ExampleCode.lean

The problem with this approach, adding a type of distance values, is that you can now have different types giving "the same" balled space structure. In valuation theory we have just spent a lot of time extracting and removing such types and instead using a preorder on the type

What about something like this?

import Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace.Defs
import Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace.Pseudo.Lemmas
import Mathlib.RingTheory.Valuation.ValuativeRel.Basic

-- The most general version of spherical completeness I can think of.
-- We probably need a better name for this...
def IsDescendingCompleteFamily {X : Type*} (𝔅 : Set (Set X)) : Prop :=
  ∀ S ⊆ 𝔅, S.Nonempty → (∀ B ∈ S, B.Nonempty) → IsChain (· ⊆ ·) S → (⋂₀ S).Nonempty

-- We move the focus from the balls to a `generalized distance function`
def IsSphericallyCompleteFun {X : Type*} {A : Type*} [Preorder A] (d : X → X → A) : Prop :=
  IsDescendingCompleteFamily {B : Set X | ∃ x r, B = {y | d x y ≤ r}}

-- Case of a (pseudo-)metric space, where we just take the standard distance function as `d`.
class PseudoMetricSpace.SphericallyCompleteSpace (X : Type*) [h : PseudoMetricSpace X] : Prop where
  sphericallyComplete : IsSphericallyCompleteFun h.dist

-- Case of ring with valuation, where we take `d` as `v(a - b)`.
class ValuativeRel.SphericallyCompleteSpace (R : Type*) [Ring R] [h : ValuativeRel R] : Prop where
  sphericallyComplete : IsSphericallyCompleteFun (fun a b => valuation R (a - b))

(This is just a proof of concept, so don't be serious about the naming issue or coding style or conditions on the variables...)

So, in this design, we have the abstraction IsDescendingCompleteFamily, where balls are just a family of subsets. I think this reflects the spirit of ball spaces. And IsSphericallyCompleteFun is a workaround for a class of generalized metric spaces.

After some thought, maybe this is not a good solution after all... If one needs to do some serious proof with IsSphericallyCompleteFun, then a raw function type d : X → X → A is far from enough. Eventually we need some type GeneralizedDist to work as a wrapper. I'm not sure whether this is a good design

I liked these solutions for the discussed use cases. What's a use case where you'd need to work with the underlying IsSphericallyCompleteFun? You could have the definition restrict the codomain to be an OrderedMonoid etc. And for the case of pseudometric spaces, you'd use the nndist or edist instead of dist, to match the constraint.

Yakov Pechersky said:

You could have the definition restrict the codomain to be an OrderedMonoid, etc. And for the case of pseudometric spaces, you'd use the nndist or edist instead of dist, to match the constraint.

The motivation of IsSphericallyCompleteFun is to abstract the spherical completeness in any space that is equipped with a "distance-like function". In the ideal scenario, if a result about spherical completeness works for both metric spaces and valued fields, then one should expect a formalized theorem that states this result with IsSphericallyCompleteFun (plus some necessary conditions).

There is no doubt that we can make the codomain an OrderedMonoid, but we may need something more (e.g., the triangle inequality) to make IsSphericallyCompleteFun really useful. For the triangle inequality, it is not possible to be wrapped into the type of A alone. So eventually it may lead to some kind of generalized metric space -- the headache that we are already aware of.

We have bundled docs#PseudoMetric which is already a bundled generalized version of what gets used in metric spaces. Note that the arguments for it require no "compatibility" of the algebra and the order. But proofs about it do. Keep the IsSpCFun prop the way it is, but for proofs about it, have that d is a bundled foo func. So this is the "state generally, prove in narrower context" pattern.

Wow, I didn't realize the existence of docs#PseudoMetric. Now my question is: is there a reason that we need the generality of IsSpCFun for raw function type d : X → X → A? I can hardly imagine any mathematical meaning of IsSpCFun for functions other than (pseudo-)metric.

I am not familiar with the ball spaces that aren't of the metric or valuation settings, so I don't know if they can always be interpreted as a generalized pseudometric. An arbitrary function I guess could be made if you have an indexed family of balls, and the d x y is the set of balls both are in, or the smallest or the intersection, etc. Zero would be the empty set, LE is subset or similar. But what would addition be? Can there be a common zero -- what would the general result be for not connected x, y under d x x and d y y?

Based on the fact that it's not clear to me how to do it, I agree with you that we can keep spherical completeness limited to pseudometrics for now, likely a predicate named PseudoMetric.SphericallyComplete, to take advantage of dot notation.
